newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thousands of miners retreat from Bonn before talks.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of miners retreat from Bonn before talks.

text.p: Thousands of angry German miners who paralysed Bonn's government district for three days to protest against planned subsidy cuts retreated on Wednesday to clear the way for Chancellor Helmut Kohl to meet union leaders.

About 6,500 miners from Saar state on the French border held a raucous rally in Bonn to fight cuts which they say will cost 50,000 jobs, but most said they would heed union calls to spend Thursday morning in nearby Cologne.

There were some hints of compromise as Kohl said he saw chances of an agreement and coalition sources said they were considering improving short-term welfare benefits for miners to ease the pain of the cuts.

Kohl had called off the crisis talks at short notice on Tuesday because of the threat of violence, and said he would meet miners' leaders on Thursday (eds: 0800 GMT) only if the protests in Bonn stopped.

"If we all stay here, we won't get our negotiations tomorrow either," union leader Hans Berger beseeched his members hoarsely. "But if the talks do not go our way we will all be back -- 50,000, 100,000 miners!"
The brawny men shouted back defiant choruses of "We're staying here!" and "We don't want to negotiate any longer" and taunted Berger with calls of "Judas, Judas!".

But thousands of pitworkers eventually headed for Cologne in coaches and on hundreds of motor cycles, leaving the streets of Bonn's usually pristine government quarter strewn with beer bottles, cigarette butts and political leaflets.
"If we don't get a reasonable result, we'll be back and all hell will be let loose," said one miner from Saarbruecken.
The IG Bergbau union set up a tent village in the grounds of Cologne football stadium for an expected 8,000 miners.
The union said it would lay on hot food and entertainment for the men, many still clad in dusty overalls and hardhats.
Kohl said he believed the talks would succeed "with a bit of goodwill". But he insisted his plan was fair.
Miners in Germany's 18 pits walked out last Friday after Bonn said it would cut subsidies to 3.8 billion marks by 2005 instead of the 6.5 billion marks unions have proposed.

Industry sources said mining company Ruhrkohle and utility Veba had put forward a new plan suggesting the government raise its offer by an annual 650 million marks until 2000 to stave off the closure of several mines.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) also made more conciliatory noises, saying for the first time they would not continue boycotting tax reform talks with the government even if Kohl failed to make a satisfactory offer to the pit workers.
But the SPD, which rules the two main mining states, said tempers would flare if there were no concessions on Thursday.
"Then the situation will become critical," SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine, premier of Saar state, told the miners.
The free-market Free Democrats (FDP), Kohl's junior coalition partners and the main force behind the plans, hinted they could amend the timetable for phasing out the subsidies.
Miners focused their anger on the FDP by locking the party out of its offices for three days. They ended their blockade on Wednesday but left the building ringed with steel chains.
Bonn argues it can no longer afford to pay over nine billion marks a year to compensate users for a domestic coal price which is over three times the world market price.
But IG Bergbau says the plans will force 10 pits to close by 2005, make 50,000 miners redundant and cause a further 70,000 related job losses in already depressed areas.

In an unrelated protest, 8,000 construction workers marched in Berlin to protest against job losses in their stricken sector. A group smashed cabbage heads to highlight their opposition to Kohl, whose name means cabbage in German.
